claim: Hepcidin mRNA levels were approximately 30 fold lower in the adult mouse heart than in the liver.
source: Hamp mRNA levels were approximately 30 fold lower in the adult mouse heart than in the liver (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by quantitative PCR data comparing Hamp mRNA expression between heart and liver tissues shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Dietary iron manipulation altered cardiac and liver iron levels.
source: having first established that this dietary manipulation altered cardiac and liver iron levels (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by elemental iron measurements in heart and liver tissues from mice fed different iron diets, shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Hamp mRNA levels in both heart and liver were decreased by the iron-deficient diet and increased by the iron-loaded diet.
source: In both tissues, Hamp mRNA levels were decreased by the iron-deficient diet (Fe 2–5 ppm) and increased by the iron-loaded diet (Fe 5000 ppm) (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by quantitative PCR data showing Hamp mRNA expression in heart and liver under different dietary iron conditions, shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Changes in hepatic HAMP protein mirrored changes in its mRNA levels in response to dietary iron manipulation.
source: At the protein level, while changes in hepatic HAMP protein mirrored changes in its mRNA levels, cardiac HAMP protein was increased by the iron-deficient diet and unaffected by the iron-loaded diet (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemical staining for HAMP protein in liver tissues under different dietary iron conditions, shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Cardiac HAMP protein was increased by the iron-deficient diet and unaffected by the iron-loaded diet.
source: At the protein level, while changes in hepatic HAMP protein mirrored changes in its mRNA levels, cardiac HAMP protein was increased by the iron-deficient diet and unaffected by the iron-loaded diet (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemical staining for HAMP protein in heart tissues under different dietary iron conditions, shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Hamp mRNA in primary adult cardiomyocytes was increased by FAC from 4 hr of treatment.
source: Relative to control cardiomyocytes at the respective timepoint, Hamp mRNA was increased by FAC from 4 hr of treatment, and decreased by DFO at 4, 8 and 16 hr of treatment (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by quantitative PCR data from primary cardiomyocytes treated with FAC over time, shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Hamp mRNA in primary adult cardiomyocytes was decreased by DFO at 4, 8 and 16 hr of treatment.
source: Relative to control cardiomyocytes at the respective timepoint, Hamp mRNA was increased by FAC from 4 hr of treatment, and decreased by DFO at 4, 8 and 16 hr of treatment (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by quantitative PCR data from primary cardiomyocytes treated with DFO over time, shown in Figure 1C.

claim: HAMP protein in supernatants of primary cardiomyocytes was increased by DFO as early as 2 hr.
source: Relative to control cardiomyocytes at the respective timepoint, HAMP protein in supernatants was increased by DFO as early as 2 hr, but remained unchanged by FAC at all timepoints (Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by ELISA measurements of HAMP protein in supernatants of primary cardiomyocytes treated with DFO, shown in Figure 1D.

claim: HAMP protein in supernatants of primary cardiomyocytes remained unchanged by FAC at all timepoints.
source: Relative to control cardiomyocytes at the respective timepoint, HAMP protein in supernatants was increased by DFO as early as 2 hr, but remained unchanged by FAC at all timepoints (Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by ELISA measurements of HAMP protein in supernatants of primary cardiomyocytes treated with FAC, shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Furin expression is upregulated in the hearts of mice provided an iron-deficient diet.
source: Furin expression has been reported in the heart (Beaubien et al., 1995; Ichiki et al., 2013), and we also found that its expression was upregulated in the hearts of mice provided an iron-deficient diet and in cardiomyocytes treated with DFO (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by quantitative PCR data showing Furin mRNA expression in hearts of mice fed iron-deficient diet, shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2, and by prior published studies.

claim: Furin expression is upregulated in cardiomyocytes treated with DFO.
source: Furin expression has been reported in the heart (Beaubien et al., 1995; Ichiki et al., 2013), and we also found that its expression was upregulated in the hearts of mice provided an iron-deficient diet and in cardiomyocytes treated with DFO (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by quantitative PCR data showing Furin mRNA expression in primary cardiomyocytes treated with DFO, shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Furin inhibition prevents the increase in HAMP release following DFO treatment in cardiomyocytes.
source: When we measured HAMP in supernatants of cardiomyocytes treated with the Furin inhibitor decanoyl-Arg-Val-Lys-Arg-chloromethylketone (CMK), we found no increase in HAMP release following DFO treatment (Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by ELISA measurements of HAMP protein in supernatants of cardiomyocytes treated with DFO and Furin inhibitor CMK, shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Furin upregulation mediates increased HAMP secretion from iron-deficient cardiomyocytes.
source: Together, these results indicate that Furin upregulation mediates increased HAMP secretion from iron-deficient cardiomyocytes.
evidence: Inferred from the combined observations that Furin is upregulated by iron deficiency, and that Furin inhibition prevents increased HAMP secretion in DFO-treated cardiomyocytes.

claim: Hamp mRNA in the hearts of Hampfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ mice was significantly reduced compared to the hearts of Hampfl/fl controls.
source: Hamp mRNA (Figure 1E) and HAMP protein (Figure 1F) in the hearts of Hampfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ mice were significantly reduced compared to the hearts of Hampfl/fl controls.
evidence: Supported by quantitative PCR data showing Hamp mRNA expression in hearts of Hampfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ mice versus controls, shown in Figure 1E.

claim: HAMP protein in the hearts of Hampfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ mice was significantly reduced compared to the hearts of Hampfl/fl controls.
source: Hamp mRNA (Figure 1E) and HAMP protein (Figure 1F) in the hearts of Hampfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ mice were significantly reduced compared to the hearts of Hampfl/fl controls.
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemical staining for HAMP protein in hearts of Hampfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ mice versus controls, shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Cardiomyocytes are the primary site of hepcidin expression in the heart.
source: Near complete ablation of the cardiac Hamp mRNA and HAMP protein in Hampfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ mice confirmed that cardiomyocytes were the primary site of hepcidin expression in the heart.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that cardiomyocyte-specific deletion of Hamp resulted in near complete ablation of cardiac Hamp mRNA and HAMP protein.

claim: Liver Hamp mRNA was not different between Hampfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ and Hampfl/fl controls.
source: Liver Hamp mRNA (Figure 1E) and HAMP protein (Figure 1F) were not different between Hampfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ and Hampfl/fl controls, consistent with the cardiac-specific nature of Hamp gene deletion.
evidence: Supported by quantitative PCR data showing Hamp mRNA expression in livers of Hampfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ mice versus controls, shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Liver HAMP protein was not different between Hampfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ and Hampfl/fl controls.
source: Liver Hamp mRNA (Figure 1E) and HAMP protein (Figure 1F) were not different between Hampfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ and Hampfl/fl controls, consistent with the cardiac-specific nature of Hamp gene deletion.
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemical staining for HAMP protein in livers of Hampfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ mice versus controls, shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Hampfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ mice had normal levels of liver iron stores and circulating markers of iron homeostasis when compared to Hampfl/fl controls.
source: Also consistent with this cardiac-specific deletion, Hampfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ mice had normal levels of liver iron stores and circulating markers of iron homeostasis when compared to Hampfl/fl controls, demonstrating that loss of cardiac hepcidin did not affect systemic iron homeostasis.
evidence: Supported by measurements of liver iron, serum iron, serum ferritin, and hemoglobin in Hampfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ mice versus controls, shown in Table 1.

claim: Loss of cardiac hepcidin did not affect systemic iron homeostasis.
source: Also consistent with this cardiac-specific deletion, Hampfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ mice had normal levels of liver iron stores and circulating markers of iron homeostasis when compared to Hampfl/fl controls, demonstrating that loss of cardiac hepcidin did not affect systemic iron homeostasis.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that Hampfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ mice had normal systemic iron indices despite cardiac-specific hepcidin deletion.

claim: Circulating HAMP levels were not reduced in the serum of Hampfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ mice.
source: In addition, circulating HAMP levels were not reduced in the serum of Hampfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ mice, suggesting that cardiac hepcidin does not contribute significantly to circulating HAMP levels (Table 1).
evidence: Supported by ELISA measurements of serum hepcidin in Hampfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ mice versus controls, shown in Table 1.

claim: Cardiac hepcidin does not contribute significantly to circulating HAMP levels.
source: In addition, circulating HAMP levels were not reduced in the serum of Hampfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ mice, suggesting that cardiac hepcidin does not contribute significantly to circulating HAMP levels (Table 1).
evidence: Inferred from the observation that serum HAMP levels were unchanged in Hampfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ mice despite cardiac-specific hepcidin deletion.

claim: Only 29% of Hampfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ mice survived to 52 weeks, compared with 90% of Hampfl/fl controls.
source: Significantly greater mortality was observed amongst Hampfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ mice, with only 29% of animals surviving to 52 weeks, compared with 90% of Hampfl/fl controls.
evidence: Supported by cumulative survival data over 52 weeks shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The median survival of Hampfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ mice was 28 weeks.
source: The median survival of Hampfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ mice was 28 weeks, whereas the majority of Hampfl/fl controls were still alive at 52 weeks (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by cumulative survival data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Six-month old Hampfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ mice showed gross enlargement of the left ventricle compared to Hampfl/fl controls.
source: Six-month old mice were sacrificed for assessment of cardiac morphology, which showed gross enlargement of the left ventricle (LV) in Hampfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ hearts compared to Hampfl/fl controls (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by H&E staining of heart sections from six-month old mice shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Hampfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ cardiomyocytes were hypertrophied.
source: Assessment of cardiomyocyte size by wheat germ agglutinin (WGA) staining confirmed that Hampfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ cardiomyocytes were hypertrophied (Figure 2C–D).
evidence: Supported by WGA staining and quantitation of cardiomyocyte size shown in Figure 2C-D.

claim: Cardiomyocyte hypertrophy in Hampfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ mice was accompanied by upregulation of expression of hypertrophic gene markers myosin heavy chain (Myh7) and natriuretic peptide precursor (Nppb).
source: This was accompanied by upregulation of expression of hypertrophic gene markers myosin heavy chain (Myh7) and natriuretic peptide precursor (Nppb) (Figure 2E).
evidence: Supported by quantitative PCR data showing Myh7 and Nppb mRNA expression in hearts of Hampfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ mice versus controls, shown in Figure 2E.

claim: TUNEL staining showed significantly greater apoptosis in the hearts of Hampfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ mice than in Hampfl/fl controls.
source: TUNEL staining for in-situ detection of cell death also showed significantly greater apoptosis in the hearts of Hampfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ mice than in Hampfl/fl controls (Figure 2F–G).
evidence: Supported by TUNEL staining and quantitation of apoptotic cardiomyocytes shown in Figure 2F-G.

claim: Cine MR images showed marked enlargement of the LV in Hampfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ mice compared to Hampfl/fl controls at 6 and 9 months of age.
source: At 6 and 9 months of age, cine MR images showed marked enlargement of the LV in Hampfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ mice compared to Hampfl/fl controls (Figure 2H).
evidence: Supported by mid-ventricular cine MR images shown in Figure 2H.

claim: Cine MRI confirmed enlargement of the LV lumen in Hampfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ mice, both at end-systole (LVES) and at end-diastole (LVED).
source: Formal quantitation of cardiac parameters by cine MRI confirmed enlargement of the LV lumen in Hampfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ mice, both at end-systole (LVES) (Figure 2I) and at end-diastole (LVED) (Figure 2J), accompanied by a decrease in LV ejection fraction (LVEF) from 62% to 42% (Figure 2K).
evidence: Supported by cine MRI measurements of LVES and LVED shown in Figure 2I-J.

claim: LV ejection fraction (LVEF) decreased from 62% to 42% in Hampfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ mice.
source: Formal quantitation of cardiac parameters by cine MRI confirmed enlargement of the LV lumen in Hampfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ mice, both at end-systole (LVES) (Figure 2I) and at end-diastole (LVED) (Figure 2J), accompanied by a decrease in LV ejection fraction (LVEF) from 62% to 42% (Figure 2K).
evidence: Supported by cine MRI measurements of LVEF shown in Figure 2K.

claim: Hampfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ mice developed fatal LV dysfunction with reduced LVEF.
source: Taken together, histological examination of the hearts and cine MRI studies indicated that Hampfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ mice developed fatal LV dysfunction with reduced LVEF.
evidence: Inferred from the combined observations of increased mortality, LV enlargement, cardiomyocyte hypertrophy, increased apoptosis, and reduced LVEF in Hampfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ mice.

claim: FPN protein was markedly upregulated in the hearts of Hampfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ mice compared to Hampfl/fl controls.
source: We examined FPN protein in the hearts of Hampfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ mice, and found that FPN protein was markedly upregulated compared to Hampfl/fl controls (Figure 3A), consistent with the idea that loss of cardiac HAMP was acting through upregulation of cardiomyocyte FPN.
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemical staining for FPN protein in hearts of Hampfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ mice versus controls, shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Cardiomyocyte FPN was upregulated in Slc40a1 C326Yfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ mice.
source: As seen in Hampfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ mice, cardiomyocyte FPN was indeed upregulated in Slc40a1 C326Yfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ mice (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemical staining for FPN protein in hearts of Slc40a1 C326Yfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ mice versus controls, shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Slc40a1 C326Yfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ mice had increased mortality relative to their littermate controls.
source: Like Hampfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ mice, Slc40a1 C326Yfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ mice also had increased mortality relative to their littermate controls (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by cumulative survival data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Slc40a1 C326Yfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ hearts from six month old mice showed LV enlargement.
source: Histologically, Slc40a1 C326Yfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ hearts from six month old mice also showed LV enlargement (Figure 3D), hypertrophied cardiomyocytes (Figure 3E–F), upregulation of hypertrophy markers Myh7 and Nppb (Figure 3G) and a greater degree of apoptosis compared to Slc40a1 C326Yfl/fl controls (Figure 3H–I).
evidence: Supported by H&E staining of heart sections from six-month old Slc40a1 C326Yfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ mice shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Slc40a1 C326Yfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ hearts from six month old mice showed hypertrophied cardiomyocytes.
source: Histologically, Slc40a1 C326Yfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ hearts from six month old mice also showed LV enlargement (Figure 3D), hypertrophied cardiomyocytes (Figure 3E–F), upregulation of hypertrophy markers Myh7 and Nppb (Figure 3G) and a greater degree of apoptosis compared to Slc40a1 C326Yfl/fl controls (Figure 3H–I).
evidence: Supported by WGA staining and quantitation of cardiomyocyte size in Slc40a1 C326Yfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ mice shown in Figure 3E-F.

claim: Slc40a1 C326Yfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ hearts from six month old mice showed upregulation of hypertrophy markers Myh7 and Nppb.
source: Histologically, Slc40a1 C326Yfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ hearts from six month old mice also showed LV enlargement (Figure 3D), hypertrophied cardiomyocytes (Figure 3E–F), upregulation of hypertrophy markers Myh7 and Nppb (Figure 3G) and a greater degree of apoptosis compared to Slc40a1 C326Yfl/fl controls (Figure 3H–I).
evidence: Supported by quantitative PCR data showing Myh7 and Nppb mRNA expression in hearts of Slc40a1 C326Yfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ mice versus controls, shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Slc40a1 C326Yfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ hearts from six month old mice showed a greater degree of apoptosis compared to Slc40a1 C326Yfl/fl controls.
source: Histologically, Slc40a1 C326Yfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ hearts from six month old mice also showed LV enlargement (Figure 3D), hypertrophied cardiomyocytes (Figure 3E–F), upregulation of hypertrophy markers Myh7 and Nppb (Figure 3G) and a greater degree of apoptosis compared to Slc40a1 C326Yfl/fl controls (Figure 3H–I).
evidence: Supported by TUNEL staining and quantitation of apoptotic cardiomyocytes in Slc40a1 C326Yfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ mice shown in Figure 3H-I.

claim: Slc40a1 C326Yfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ mice developed LV dysfunction by 6 months of age, with a reduction in LVEF from 73% to 55%.
source: When we measured cardiac performance by cine MRI, we found that Slc40a1 C326Yfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ mice also developed LV dysfunction by 6 months of age, with a reduction in LVEF from 73% to 55% (Figure 3J–L).
evidence: Supported by cine MRI measurements of LVES, LVED, and LVEF in Slc40a1 C326Yfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ mice versus controls shown in Figure 3J-L.

claim: Iron Fe55 efflux was significantly greater in cardiomyocytes isolated from Hampfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ and Slc40a1 C326Yfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ hearts than in cardiomyocytes isolated from their respective controls.
source: Iron Fe55 efflux was indeed significantly greater in cardiomyocytes isolated from Hampfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ and Slc40a1 C326Yfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ hearts than in cardiomyocytes isolated from their respective controls (Figure 3M).
evidence: Supported by Fe55 efflux measurements in isolated cardiomyocytes shown in Figure 3M.

claim: Addition of exogenous mouse HAMP in the efflux medium inhibited the increase in Fe55 efflux from Hampfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ cardiomyocytes but not from Slc40a1 C326Yfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ cardiomyocytes.
source: Addition of exogenous mouse HAMP in the efflux medium inhibited the increase in Fe55 efflux from Hampfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ cardiomyocytes but not from Slc40a1 C326Yfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ cardiomyocytes, consistent with the HAMP-resistant mutation in Slc40a1 C326Yfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ cardiomyocytes.
evidence: Supported by Fe55 efflux measurements in isolated cardiomyocytes treated with HAMP peptide shown in Figure 3M.

claim: The iron content of the cardiomyocyte fraction was significantly lower in Hampfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ and in Slc40a1 C326Yfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ mice than in their respective controls.
source: While iron levels in total hearts were not significantly different between any of the genotypes (Figure 3—figure supplement 2), the iron content of the cardiomyocyte fraction was significantly lower in Hampfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ and in Slc40a1 C326Yfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ mice than in their respective controls (Figure 3N).
evidence: Supported by ICP-MS measurements of elemental iron in isolated cardiomyocyte fractions shown in Figure 3N.

claim: Expression of TfR1 mRNA was upregulated in Hampfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ and Slc40a1 C326Yfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ hearts relative to their respective controls.
source: Furthermore, expression of TfR1 mRNA was upregulated (Figure 3O) and Slc40a1 mRNA was downregulated (Figure 3P) in Hampfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ and Slc40a1 C326Yfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ hearts relative to their respective controls, consistent with a transcriptional response to intracellular iron deficiency (Rouault and Klausner, 1997; Rouault, 2006; Ward and Kaplan, 1823).
evidence: Supported by quantitative PCR data showing TfR1 mRNA expression in hearts of Hampfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ and Slc40a1 C326Yfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ mice versus controls, shown in Figure 3O, and by prior published studies on iron regulatory mechanisms.

claim: Slc40a1 mRNA was downregulated in Hampfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ and Slc40a1 C326Yfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ hearts relative to their respective controls.
source: Furthermore, expression of TfR1 mRNA was upregulated (Figure 3O) and Slc40a1 mRNA was downregulated (Figure 3P) in Hampfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ and Slc40a1 C326Yfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ hearts relative to their respective controls, consistent with a transcriptional response to intracellular iron deficiency (Rouault and Klausner, 1997; Rouault, 2006; Ward and Kaplan, 1823).
evidence: Supported by quantitative PCR data showing Slc40a1 mRNA expression in hearts of Hampfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ and Slc40a1 C326Yfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ mice versus controls, shown in Figure 3P, and by prior published studies on iron regulatory mechanisms.

claim: Loss of either cardiac hepcidin or hepcidin responsiveness in the heart results in upregulation of cardiomyocyte FPN.
source: Together these results demonstrate that loss of either cardiac hepcidin or hepcidin responsiveness in the heart results in upregulation of cardiomyocyte FPN, and that cardiomyocytes of Hampfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ and Slc40a1 C326Yfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ hearts are iron deficient as a result of upregulation of FPN-mediated iron export.
evidence: Inferred from the combined observations that both Hampfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ and Slc40a1 C326Yfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ mice show upregulated FPN protein in the heart.

claim: Cardiomyocytes of Hampfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ and Slc40a1 C326Yfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ hearts are iron deficient as a result of upregulation of FPN-mediated iron export.
source: Together these results demonstrate that loss of either cardiac hepcidin or hepcidin responsiveness in the heart results in upregulation of cardiomyocyte FPN, and that cardiomyocytes of Hampfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ and Slc40a1 C326Yfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ hearts are iron deficient as a result of upregulation of FPN-mediated iron export.
evidence: Inferred from the combined observations of increased Fe55 efflux, decreased cardiomyocyte iron content, and upregulation of iron deficiency markers in both mouse models.

claim: The LV enlargement and the reduced LVEF, seen in untreated Hampfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ mice, were prevented in iron-treated Hampfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ mice.
source: At this timepoint, we performed cine MRI and found that the LV enlargement and the reduced LVEF, seen in untreated Hampfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ mice, were prevented in iron-treated Hampfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ mice (Figure 4A–C).
evidence: Supported by cine MRI measurements of LVES, LVED, and LVEF in untreated and iron-treated Hampfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ mice shown in Figure 4A-C.

claim: The transcriptional response to intracellular iron deficiency in untreated Hampfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ mice was absent in iron-treated Hampfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ mice.
source: The transcriptional response to intracellular iron deficiency in untreated Hampfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ mice (upregulation of TfR1 mRNA and downregulation of Slc40a1 mRNA relative to Hampfl/fl controls), was absent in iron-treated Hampfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ mice, consistent with correction of cardiomyocyte iron deficiency (Figure 4D–E).
evidence: Supported by quantitative PCR data showing TfR1 and Slc40a1 mRNA expression in untreated and iron-treated Hampfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ mice shown in Figure 4D-E.

claim: Prevention of cardiac dysfunction in Hampfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ mice by intravenous iron treatment confirms the causal relationship between cardiomyocyte iron deficiency and cardiac dysfunction.
source: Prevention of cardiac dysfunction in Hampfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ mice by intravenous iron treatment confirms the causal relationship between cardiomyocyte iron deficiency and cardiac dysfunction in this setting.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that iron supplementation prevented cardiac dysfunction in Hampfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ mice.

claim: Aconitase I activity was significantly reduced in Hampfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ hearts compared to Hampfl/fl controls at 3 months and 6 months of age.
source: We found that Aconitase I, Complex I and Complex IV activities were significantly reduced in Hampfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ hearts compared to Hampfl/fl controls at 3 months and 6 months of age, and that this reduction in activity was prevented in iron-treated 6-month old mice (Figure 4F–H).
evidence: Supported by enzymatic activity assays for Aconitase I in hearts of Hampfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ mice versus controls shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Complex I activity was significantly reduced in Hampfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ hearts compared to Hampfl/fl controls at 3 months and 6 months of age.
source: We found that Aconitase I, Complex I and Complex IV activities were significantly reduced in Hampfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ hearts compared to Hampfl/fl controls at 3 months and 6 months of age, and that this reduction in activity was prevented in iron-treated 6-month old mice (Figure 4F–H).
evidence: Supported by enzymatic activity assays for Complex I in hearts of Hampfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ mice versus controls shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Complex IV activity was significantly reduced in Hampfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ hearts compared to Hampfl/fl controls at 3 months and 6 months of age.
source: We found that Aconitase I, Complex I and Complex IV activities were significantly reduced in Hampfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ hearts compared to Hampfl/fl controls at 3 months and 6 months of age, and that this reduction in activity was prevented in iron-treated 6-month old mice (Figure 4F–H).
evidence: Supported by enzymatic activity assays for Complex IV in hearts of Hampfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ mice versus controls shown in Figure 4H.

claim: The reduction in activity of Aconitase I, Complex I and Complex IV was prevented in iron-treated 6-month old Hampfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ mice.
source: We found that Aconitase I, Complex I and Complex IV activities were significantly reduced in Hampfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ hearts compared to Hampfl/fl controls at 3 months and 6 months of age, and that this reduction in activity was prevented in iron-treated 6-month old mice (Figure 4F–H).
evidence: Supported by enzymatic activity assays in iron-treated Hampfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ mice shown in Figure 4F-H.

claim: Dilation of mitochondrial cristae was seen in Hampfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ hearts as early as 3 months of age and progressed further at 6 months of age.
source: By electron microscopy (EM), dilation of mitochondrial cristae was seen in Hampfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ hearts as early as 3 months of age and progressed further at 6 months of age.
evidence: Supported by electron microscopy images of hearts from Hampfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ mice at 3 and 6 months shown in Figure 4I.

claim: Mitochondrial cristae dilation was prevented in iron-treated Hampfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ mice, which had healthy-looking mitochondria at 6 months of age.
source: However, this was prevented in iron-treated Hampfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ mice, which had healthy-looking mitochondria at 6 months of age (Figure 4I).
evidence: Supported by electron microscopy images of hearts from iron-treated Hampfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ mice shown in Figure 4I.

claim: Expression of genes encoding Hexokinase 2 (Hk2), Enolase (Eno), and Lactate dehydrogenase A (Ldha) were all significantly increased at 3 months and 6 months of age in hearts of untreated Hampfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ mice.
source: We found that expression of genes encoding Hexokinase 2 (Hk2) which catalyses the first step of glycolysis, Enolase (Eno), which catalyses the penultimate step of glycolysis and of Lactate dehydrogenase A (Ldha) which catalyses the ultimate step of glycolysis were all significantly increased at 3 months and 6 months of age in hearts of untreated Hampfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ mice.
evidence: Supported by quantitative PCR data showing Hk2, Eno, and Ldha mRNA expression in hearts of untreated Hampfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ mice versus controls shown in Figure 4J-L.

claim: Upregulation of glycolytic genes was not seen in iron-treated Hampfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ mice.
source: This upregulation of glycolytic genes was not seen in iron-treated Hampfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ mice (Figure 4J–L).
evidence: Supported by quantitative PCR data showing Hk2, Eno, and Ldha mRNA expression in iron-treated Hampfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ mice shown in Figure 4J-L.

claim: Reduction in the activities of key iron-containing metabolic enzymes, mitochondrial failure and upregulated glycolysis precede the development of cardiac dysfunction in Hampfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ hearts.
source: These results demonstrate that reduction in the activities of key iron-containing metabolic enzymes, mitochondrial failure and upregulated glycolysis precede the development of cardiac dysfunction in Hampfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ hearts, and are prevented by intravenous iron treatment.
evidence: Inferred from the temporal sequence of observations showing metabolic changes at 3 months and cardiac dysfunction at 6 months in Hampfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ mice.

claim: Reduction in the activities of key iron-containing metabolic enzymes, mitochondrial failure and upregulated glycolysis are prevented by intravenous iron treatment in Hampfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ hearts.
source: These results demonstrate that reduction in the activities of key iron-containing metabolic enzymes, mitochondrial failure and upregulated glycolysis precede the development of cardiac dysfunction in Hampfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ hearts, and are prevented by intravenous iron treatment.
evidence: Supported by the combined observations that iron treatment prevented reductions in enzyme activities, mitochondrial abnormalities, and upregulation of glycolytic genes.

claim: Cardiomyocyte hepcidin is required for autonomous cellular iron homeostasis.
source: The major finding of this study is that cardiomyocyte hepcidin is required for autonomous cellular iron homeostasis.
evidence: Inferred from the combined observations that loss of cardiac hepcidin leads to cardiomyocyte iron deficiency despite normal systemic iron homeostasis.

claim: Cardiac hepcidin operates in an autocrine fashion by regulating cardiomyocyte FPN.
source: Loss of hepcidin responsiveness specifically in cardiomyocytes engendered the same effects as loss of cardiac hepcidin, demonstrating that cardiac hepcidin operates in an autocrine fashion by regulating cardiomyocyte FPN.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that both cardiac hepcidin deletion and cardiac FPN mutation resistant to hepcidin produce similar phenotypes.

claim: A role in cellular iron homeostasis, and an autocrine mode of action for the HAMP/FPN axis have not been described previously in any other tissue.
source: A role in cellular iron homeostasis, and an autocrine mode of action for the HAMP/FPN axis have not been described previously in any other tissue.
evidence: Based on the authors' knowledge of the existing scientific literature on hepcidin and ferroportin function.

claim: The cardiac HAMP/FPN axis is essential for normal heart function.
source: A second important finding is that this cardiac HAMP/FPN axis is essential for normal heart function, and that its disruption leads to ultimately fatal cardiac metabolic and contractile dysfunction, even against a background of intact systemic iron homeostasis.
evidence: Inferred from the observations that disruption of the cardiac HAMP/FPN axis leads to cardiac dysfunction and increased mortality despite normal systemic iron indices.

claim: Disruption of the cardiac HAMP/FPN axis leads to ultimately fatal cardiac metabolic and contractile dysfunction, even against a background of intact systemic iron homeostasis.
source: A second important finding is that this cardiac HAMP/FPN axis is essential for normal heart function, and that its disruption leads to ultimately fatal cardiac metabolic and contractile dysfunction, even against a background of intact systemic iron homeostasis.
evidence: Supported by the combined observations of increased mortality, cardiac dysfunction, and metabolic abnormalities in Hampfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ and Slc40a1 C326Yfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ mice despite normal systemic iron indices.

claim: Metabolic and contractile dysfunction are preceded by cardiomyocyte iron deficiency and prevented by intravenous iron supplementation.
source: Metabolic and contractile dysfunction are preceded by cardiomyocyte iron deficiency and prevented by intravenous iron supplementation, indicating a causal relationship between cardiomyocyte iron deficiency and cardiac dysfunction.
evidence: Supported by the temporal sequence of observations and the prevention of dysfunction by iron treatment.

claim: There is a causal relationship between cardiomyocyte iron deficiency and cardiac dysfunction.
source: Metabolic and contractile dysfunction are preceded by cardiomyocyte iron deficiency and prevented by intravenous iron supplementation, indicating a causal relationship between cardiomyocyte iron deficiency and cardiac dysfunction.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that iron supplementation prevents cardiac dysfunction in Hampfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ mice.

claim: Cardiomyocytes secrete an active HAMP peptide in a Furin-dependent manner.
source: We found that Furin inhibition increased iron export from Hampfl/fl but not from Hampfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ cardiomyocytes (Appendix 1—figure 1), demonstrating that cardiomyocytes secrete an active HAMP peptide in a Furin-dependent manner.
evidence: Supported by Fe55 efflux experiments in cardiomyocytes treated with Furin inhibitor, referenced in Appendix 1—figure 1.

claim: Differential regulation of Furin by iron may explain the divergent effects of iron on Hamp transcript and HAMP protein.
source: These data suggest that differential regulation of Furin by iron may explain the divergent effects of iron on Hamp transcript and HAMP protein.
evidence: Speculative inference based on the observed upregulation of Furin by iron deficiency and its role in HAMP secretion.

claim: Upregulation of cardiac HAMP in mice fed an iron-deficient diet raises the possibility that it may be involved in protecting the heart in the setting of systemic iron deficiency.
source: The upregulation of cardiac HAMP in mice fed an iron-deficient diet raises the possibility that it may be involved in protecting the heart in the setting of systemic iron deficiency.
evidence: Speculative inference based on the observation that cardiac HAMP protein is increased by iron-deficient diet.

claim: When provided an iron-deficient diet, Hampfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ mice exhibited a greater cardiac hypertrophic response than their Hampfl/fl littermate controls.
source: This hypothesis is supported by the finding that, when provided an iron-deficient diet, Hampfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ mice exhibited a greater cardiac hypertrophic response than their Hampfl/fl littermate controls (Appendix 1—figure 2).
evidence: Supported by data referenced in Appendix 1—figure 2 showing cardiac hypertrophic response in Hampfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ mice on iron-deficient diet.

claim: Ubiquitous Hamp knockout and ubiquitous Slc40a1 C326Y knock-in mice do not develop the cardiac dysfunction seen in cardiomyocyte-specific Hamp knockout and cardiomyocyte-specific Slc40a1 C326Y knock-in mice.
source: It is interesting that ubiquitous Hamp knockout (Lakhal-Littleton et al., 2015) and ubiquitous Slc40a1 C326Y knock-in mice (Appendix 1—figure 3), both models of systemic iron overload, do not develop the cardiac dysfunction seen in cardiomyocyte-specific Hamp knockout and cardiomyocyte-specific Slc40a1 C326Y knock-in mice.
evidence: Supported by comparison with prior published data on ubiquitous Hamp knockout mice and data on ubiquitous Slc40a1 C326Y knock-in mice referenced in Appendix 1—figure 3.

claim: Upregulation of cardiomyocyte FPN under conditions of normal iron availability is detrimental to cardiac function.
source: This suggests that, while upregulation of cardiomyocyte FPN under conditions of normal iron availability (cardiac-specific models described in this study) is detrimental to cardiac function, it is protective under conditions of increased systemic iron availability (systemic models).
evidence: Inferred from the comparison between cardiac-specific and systemic models of FPN upregulation.

claim: Upregulation of cardiomyocyte FPN is protective under conditions of increased systemic iron availability.
source: This suggests that, while upregulation of cardiomyocyte FPN under conditions of normal iron availability (cardiac-specific models described in this study) is detrimental to cardiac function, it is protective under conditions of increased systemic iron availability (systemic models).
evidence: Inferred from the observation that systemic models with iron overload do not develop cardiac dysfunction despite FPN upregulation.

claim: Deletion of cardiomyocyte FPN resulted in fatal cardiomyocyte iron overload, preventable by dietary iron restriction.
source: Previously, we also showed that deletion of cardiomyocyte FPN resulted in fatal cardiomyocyte iron overload, preventable by dietary iron restriction (Lakhal-Littleton et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by prior published work by the authors cited in the manuscript.

claim: Iron levels within cardiomyocytes are a balance between cellular iron efflux which is regulated by the cardiac HAMP/FPN axis, and systemic iron availability which is regulated by the systemic HAMP/FPN axis.
source: Together, our studies demonstrate that iron levels within cardiomyocytes are a balance between cellular iron efflux which is regulated by the cardiac HAMP/FPN axis, and systemic iron availability which is regulated by the systemic HAMP/FPN axis (Figure 5).
evidence: Inferred from the combined observations across different mouse models showing the interplay between cardiac and systemic iron regulation, illustrated in Figure 5.

claim: Iron overload is detrimental to cardiac health, as demonstrated by iron overload cardiomyopathy in hemochromatosis and thalassemia major patients.
source: Iron overload is detrimental to cardiac health, as demonstrated by iron overload cardiomyopathy in hemochromatosis and thalassemia major patients (Gulati et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by prior published clinical studies on iron overload cardiomyopathy.

claim: The cardiac HAMP/FPN axis may have a modifying effect on the severity of iron-overload cardiomyopathy.
source: Our model of cardiac iron homeostasis implies that the cardiac HAMP/FPN axis may have a modifying effect on the severity of iron-overload cardiomyopathy.
evidence: Speculative inference based on the proposed model of cardiac iron homeostasis.

claim: There is a lack of concordance between the degrees of cardiac iron overload and liver iron overload in a significant proportion of hemochromatosis and thalassemia major patients.
source: Thus, it would be interesting to explore whether differences in the levels of cardiac FPN and HAMP, possibly due to different local stimulatory and suppressive signals (e.g local inflammation, local ischemia), explain the reported lack of concordance between the degrees of cardiac iron overload and liver iron overload in a significant proportion of hemochromatosis and thalassemia major patients (Anderson et al., 2001; Noetzli et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by prior published clinical studies on iron overload in hemochromatosis and thalassemia patients.

claim: Systemic iron deficiency correlates with functional and molecular markers of disease severity in patients with chronic heart failure (CHF).
source: Indeed, systemic iron deficiency correlates with functional and molecular markers of disease severity in patients with chronic heart failure (CHF) (Klip et al., 2013; Comín-Colet et al., 2013),and also appears to contribute to the risk of death after an episode of acute heart failure (Jankowska et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by prior published clinical studies on iron deficiency in heart failure patients.

claim: Iron deficiency appears to contribute to the risk of death after an episode of acute heart failure.
source: Indeed, systemic iron deficiency correlates with functional and molecular markers of disease severity in patients with chronic heart failure (CHF) (Klip et al., 2013; Comín-Colet et al., 2013),and also appears to contribute to the risk of death after an episode of acute heart failure (Jankowska et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by prior published clinical studies on iron deficiency and mortality in heart failure patients.

claim: The prevalence of iron deficiency in patients with CHF ranges between 30–50%.
source: Given the high prevalence of iron deficiency in patients with CHF, ranging between 30–50% (Klip et al., 2013; Nanas et al., 2006; Ezekowitz et al., 2003), the European Society of Cardiology recently recommended the assessment of iron deficiency as a comorbidity in CHF.
evidence: Supported by prior published clinical studies on the prevalence of iron deficiency in heart failure patients.

claim: The European Society of Cardiology recently recommended the assessment of iron deficiency as a comorbidity in CHF.
source: Given the high prevalence of iron deficiency in patients with CHF, ranging between 30–50% (Klip et al., 2013; Nanas et al., 2006; Ezekowitz et al., 2003), the European Society of Cardiology recently recommended the assessment of iron deficiency as a comorbidity in CHF.
evidence: Based on established clinical guidelines from the European Society of Cardiology.

claim: Several clinical trials have established the benefits of intravenous iron supplementation in CHF patients, with or without anaemia.
source: Furthermore, several clinical trials have now established the benefits of intravenous iron supplementation in CHF patients, with or without anaemia (Ponikowski et al., 2015; Anker et al., 2009; Avni et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by prior published clinical trials on iron supplementation in heart failure patients.

claim: The mechanisms underlying the anaemia-independent effects of iron deficiency and the benefits of intravenous iron in CHF patients are not fully understood.
source: The mechanisms underlying the anaemia-independent effects of iron deficiency and the benefits of intravenous iron in CHF patients are not fully understood.
evidence: Based on the authors' knowledge of the current state of understanding in the field.

claim: Hamp mRNA and HAMP protein are elevated in the ischemic myocardium during the acute phase in the rat model of myocardial infarction (MI).
source: It has been shown, in the rat model of myocardial infarction (MI), that Hamp mRNA and HAMP protein are elevated in the ischemic myocardium during the acute phase (Simonis et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by prior published studies in rat models of myocardial infarction.

claim: Circulating HAMP was shown to be elevated in the serum within 4 hr of MI in humans.
source: In humans, circulating HAMP was shown to be elevated in the serum within 4 hr of MI, although the tissue source of this hepcidin was not identified (Suzuki et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by prior published clinical studies on hepcidin levels in myocardial infarction patients.

claim: Decreased cardiac HAMP expression has been reported in a transgenic mouse model of dilated cardiomyopathy.
source: In addition, decreased cardiac HAMP expression has been reported in a transgenic mouse model of dilated cardiomyopathy, where the phenotype was ameliorated following transgenic overexpression of cardiac hepcidin (Zhang et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by prior published studies in mouse models of dilated cardiomyopathy.

claim: The phenotype of dilated cardiomyopathy in a transgenic mouse model was ameliorated following transgenic overexpression of cardiac hepcidin.
source: In addition, decreased cardiac HAMP expression has been reported in a transgenic mouse model of dilated cardiomyopathy, where the phenotype was ameliorated following transgenic overexpression of cardiac hepcidin (Zhang et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by prior published studies in mouse models of dilated cardiomyopathy.

claim: Strategies that target the HAMP/FPN axis may impinge on cardiac iron homeostasis and function.
source: Currently, there is considerable interest in targeting the HAMP/FPN axis for the treatment of iron overload and iron deficiency. Our studies suggest that such strategies may also impinge on cardiac iron homeostasis and function.
evidence: Speculative inference based on the findings that cardiac HAMP/FPN axis is important for cardiac iron homeostasis and function.

claim: Both FPN and hepcidin are found in the brain, kidney and placenta.
source: Other than the heart, both FPN and hepcidin are also found in the brain, kidney and placenta (McCarthy and Kosman, 2014; Kulaksiz, 2005; Evans et al., 2011; Rouault, 2013; Moos and Rosengren Nielsen, 2006; Bastin et al., 2006; Wolff et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by prior published studies on FPN and hepcidin expression in various tissues.

claim: Hepcidin is the master regulator of systemic iron homeostasis.
source: Hepcidin is the master regulator of systemic iron homeostasis.
evidence: Based on established scientific consensus on hepcidin's role in iron homeostasis.

claim: Hepcidin is derived primarily from the liver.
source: Derived primarily from the liver, it inhibits the iron exporter ferroportin in the gut and spleen, the sites of iron absorption and recycling respectively.
evidence: Based on established scientific consensus on the primary source of hepcidin.

claim: Hepcidin inhibits the iron exporter ferroportin in the gut and spleen, the sites of iron absorption and recycling respectively.
source: Derived primarily from the liver, it inhibits the iron exporter ferroportin in the gut and spleen, the sites of iron absorption and recycling respectively.
evidence: Based on established scientific consensus on hepcidin's mechanism of action.

claim: Ferroportin is found in cardiomyocytes.
source: Recently, we demonstrated that ferroportin is also found in cardiomyocytes, and that its cardiac-specific deletion leads to fatal cardiac iron overload.
evidence: Supported by prior published work by the authors.

claim: Cardiac-specific deletion of ferroportin leads to fatal cardiac iron overload.
source: Recently, we demonstrated that ferroportin is also found in cardiomyocytes, and that its cardiac-specific deletion leads to fatal cardiac iron overload.
evidence: Supported by prior published work by the authors.

claim: Hepcidin is expressed in cardiomyocytes.
source: Hepcidin is also expressed in cardiomyocytes, where its function remains unknown.
evidence: Based on the authors' prior observations and established knowledge.

claim: The function of hepcidin in cardiomyocytes remains unknown.
source: Hepcidin is also expressed in cardiomyocytes, where its function remains unknown.
evidence: Based on the state of knowledge prior to this study.

claim: Both models (Hampfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ and Slc40a1 C326Yfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+) maintain normal systemic iron homeostasis.
source: We find that while both models maintain normal systemic iron homeostasis, they nonetheless develop fatal contractile and metabolic dysfunction as a consequence of cardiomyocyte iron deficiency.
evidence: Supported by measurements of systemic iron indices in both mouse models shown in Tables 1 and 3.

claim: Both models (Hampfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ and Slc40a1 C326Yfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+) develop fatal contractile and metabolic dysfunction as a consequence of cardiomyocyte iron deficiency.
source: We find that while both models maintain normal systemic iron homeostasis, they nonetheless develop fatal contractile and metabolic dysfunction as a consequence of cardiomyocyte iron deficiency.
evidence: Supported by the combined observations of increased mortality, cardiac dysfunction, metabolic abnormalities, and cardiomyocyte iron deficiency in both mouse models.

claim: These findings are the first demonstration of a cell-autonomous role for hepcidin in iron homeostasis.
source: These findings are the first demonstration of a cell-autonomous role for hepcidin in iron homeostasis.
evidence: Based on the authors' knowledge of the existing scientific literature.

claim: The cell-autonomous function of hepcidin may also be important in other tissues that express both hepcidin and ferroportin, such as the kidney and the brain.
source: They raise the possibility that such function may also be important in other tissues that express both hepcidin and ferroportin, such as the kidney and the brain.
evidence: Speculative inference based on the findings in the heart and the known expression of hepcidin and ferroportin in other tissues.

claim: Iron is essential for cellular functions as a constituent of hemoproteins, iron-sulphur proteins and other functional groups.
source: As a constituent of hemoproteins, iron-sulphur proteins and other functional groups, iron is essential for cellular functions.
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge about iron's role in cellular biochemistry.

claim: Excess iron participates in cytotoxic Fenton-type chemical reactions.
source: Conversely, excess iron participates in cytotoxic Fenton-type chemical reactions.
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge about iron chemistry and toxicity.

claim: Both iron deficiency and iron overload are detrimental to the cell.
source: Thus, both iron deficiency and iron overload are detrimental to the cell.
evidence: Inferred from the established knowledge that iron is essential but excess iron is toxic.

claim: Cellular iron homeostasis is controlled by the Iron Regulatory Proteins IRPs.
source: In mammals, cellular iron homeostasis is controlled by the Iron Regulatory Proteins IRPs.
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge about cellular iron regulation.

claim: Intracellular iron levels control the degradation of IRP2 and the conformational switch that confers the RNA-binding function of IRP1.
source: Intracellular iron levels control the degradation of IRP2 and the conformational switch that confers the RNA-binding function of IRP1.
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge about IRP regulation.

claim: IRPs control the levels of iron uptake proteins such as transferrin receptor 1 (TfR1) and divalent metal transporter (DMT1), and the iron storage protein ferritin.
source: IRPs in turn control the levels of iron uptake proteins such as transferrin receptor 1 (TfR1) and divalent metal transporter (DMT1), and the iron storage protein ferritin (Rouault and Klausner, 1997; Rouault, 2006).
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge about IRP function, supported by cited references.

claim: Systemic iron homeostasis is controlled by the hepcidin/ferroportin axis at the sites of iron entry into the circulation.
source: Systemic iron homeostasis is controlled by the hepcidin/ferroportin axis at the sites of iron entry into the circulation.
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge about systemic iron regulation.

claim: Ferroportin (FPN) is the only known mammalian iron export protein.
source: Ferroportin (FPN), which is encoded by the Solute Carrier Family 40 Member 1 (Slc40a1), is the only known mammalian iron export protein and mediates iron release into the circulation from duodenal enterocytes, splenic reticuloendothelial macrophages and hepatocytes, the sites of iron absorption, recycling and storage respectively (Ganz, 2005; Donovan et al., 2005).
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge about ferroportin, supported by cited references.

claim: FPN mediates iron release into the circulation from duodenal enterocytes, splenic reticuloendothelial macrophages and hepatocytes.
source: Ferroportin (FPN), which is encoded by the Solute Carrier Family 40 Member 1 (Slc40a1), is the only known mammalian iron export protein and mediates iron release into the circulation from duodenal enterocytes, splenic reticuloendothelial macrophages and hepatocytes, the sites of iron absorption, recycling and storage respectively (Ganz, 2005; Donovan et al., 2005).
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge about ferroportin function, supported by cited references.

claim: FPN-mediated iron release is antagonized by the hormone hepcidin.
source: FPN-mediated iron release is antagonized by the hormone hepcidin, also known as hepcidin antimicrobial peptide (HAMP).
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge about hepcidin-ferroportin interaction.

claim: Hepcidin is produced primarily in the liver.
source: Produced primarily in the liver, hepcidin binds to and induces internalization of FPN, thereby limiting iron release into the circulation and its availability to peripheral tissues (Nemeth et al., 2004; Qiao et al., 2012).
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge about hepcidin production, supported by cited references.

claim: Hepcidin binds to and induces internalization of FPN, thereby limiting iron release into the circulation and its availability to peripheral tissues.
source: Produced primarily in the liver, hepcidin binds to and induces internalization of FPN, thereby limiting iron release into the circulation and its availability to peripheral tissues (Nemeth et al., 2004; Qiao et al., 2012).
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge about hepcidin mechanism of action, supported by cited references.

claim: Hepcidin production is impaired in diseases of systemic iron overload such as hemochromatosis and β-thalassaemia.
source: The importance of the HAMP/FPN axis is illustrated by diseases of systemic iron overload such as hemochromatosis and β-thalassaemia, where hepcidin production is impaired (Camaschella, 2005; Musallam et al., 2012), and in anaemia of chronic disease where hepcidin production is inappropriately elevated (De Falco et al., 2013; Nemeth and Ganz, 2014).
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge about hepcidin dysregulation in disease, supported by cited references.

claim: Hepcidin production is inappropriately elevated in anaemia of chronic disease.
source: The importance of the HAMP/FPN axis is illustrated by diseases of systemic iron overload such as hemochromatosis and β-thalassaemia, where hepcidin production is impaired (Camaschella, 2005; Musallam et al., 2012), and in anaemia of chronic disease where hepcidin production is inappropriately elevated (De Falco et al., 2013; Nemeth and Ganz, 2014).
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge about hepcidin dysregulation in disease, supported by cited references.

claim: Hepcidin is found in tissues with no recognized role in systemic iron homeostasis, including the heart, the brain, the kidney and the placenta.
source: Other than the liver, hepcidin is also found in tissues with no recognized role in systemic iron homeostasis, including the heart (Merle et al., 2007), the brain (McCarthy and Kosman, 2014), the kidney (Kulaksiz, 2005) and the placenta (Evans et al., 2011).
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge about extra-hepatic hepcidin expression, supported by cited references.

claim: The function of extra-hepatic hepcidin remains unknown.
source: The function of this extra-hepatic hepcidin remains unknown, but one hypothesis is that it is involved in local iron control.
evidence: Based on the state of knowledge prior to this study.

claim: One hypothesis is that extra-hepatic hepcidin is involved in local iron control.
source: The function of this extra-hepatic hepcidin remains unknown, but one hypothesis is that it is involved in local iron control.
evidence: Speculative hypothesis based on the expression pattern of hepcidin.
